steps.action: Cite the Chilean–Mariana subduction-style classification, whose regression on slab age and convergence rate predicts a maximum IBM magnitude below about Mw 7.6.
steps.quote: the predicted maximum earthquake magnitude according to the Chilean–Mariana subduction style classification paradigm is even smaller, possibly less than Mw 7.6

steps.action: Report that Cascadia 1700, Sumatra 2004 and Tohoku 2011, as established by other groups, refuted the classification's maximum-magnitude predictions.
steps.quote: provided direct refutations of the predictions from this classification scheme

steps.action: Cite McCaffrey's (2008) size-based expectation of Mw 9.2 (Izu) and Mw 9.5 (Mariana), with recurrence intervals of 723 and 893 years.
steps.quote: this approach yields a value of Mw 9.2 for the Izu segment and Mw 9.5 for the Mariana segment

steps.action: Pose the question of which Pacific Basin locations would have recorded the far-field tsunami of a great IBM earthquake, and whether the historical record shows any such tsunami.
steps.quote: which areas of the Pacific Basin would be most likely to have recorded the effects of the ensuing tsunami?

steps.action: Summarize the instrumental and historical IBM earthquake and tsunami catalogue from published sources: the largest event is Mw 7.8, 1993; tsunamis occurred in 1826, 1849, 1872 and 1892.
steps.quote: The earliest tsunami attributable to an earthquake from the Izu–Bonin–Mariana arc is likely the earthquake and tsunami of January 1826

steps.action: Design the scenario set: three strike-based segments on the NOAA SIFT geometry, three Gaussian-like slip sources each (Mw 8.7, 9.0, 9.3), and 23 gauges chosen for long written tsunami records in water shallower than 20 m.
steps.quote: In choosing circum-Pacific locations for forward modeling, we endeavored to select locations with known written records of past tsunami.

steps.action: Run the nine scenarios in GeoClaw 5.7 with adjoint-guided adaptive mesh refinement on GEBCO 2019 bathymetry (1° to 30 arcsec) and extract water-height time series at the gauges.
steps.quote: Tsunami simulations were then performed using GeoClaw 5.7 (Clawpack Development Team 1) with grid refinement guided by the adjoint method

steps.action: Check the non-dispersive GeoClaw premise with Shuto's Eq. (1) and with dispersive JAGURS runs at Kochi, Tanabe and Miho (Figure S4), concluding that GeoClaw maxima are a worst case at far gauges.
steps.quote: preliminary modeling using JAGURS (Baba et al. 4) suggests that dispersion may result in a limited reduction in amplitude

steps.action: Build an observability index (maximum wave height over GLOSS mean tidal range) and set the Unobservable/Possibly/Likely thresholds at 30% and 100% from the smallest reliable eyewitness reports in the NCEI/WDS database.
steps.quote: we have developed a basic tsunami observability index based on the relative amplitude of the largest wave with respect to the local tidal variation

steps.action: Report the predicted maximum heights and observability class per scenario and gauge: Mw 9.3 is Likely Observable nearly everywhere, Mw 9.0 is observable throughout Japan, and Mw 8.7 sits mostly near half the tidal range.
steps.quote: Earthquakes with magnitude Mw 9.3 produce tsunamis with wave heights in excess of the local tidal range at nearly all Pacific Basin locations

steps.action: Compile the earliest written tsunami record and the apparent onset of record completeness for each gauge region from catalogues (Table 1, Figure 4).
steps.quote: The number of records increases starting around 1403 indicating an improvement in the completeness of the observations for this location.

steps.action: Combine predicted observability with record completeness per segment, postulating dates after which any tsunami from an IBM source larger than Mw 8.7 (or Mw 9.0/9.3 in the Americas) should appear in the record.
steps.quote: we postulate that records of any tsunami from an earthquake greater than Mw 8.7 from an Izu–Bonin source after 1403

steps.action: Take up Harada et al.'s (2013) proposal that the 1605 Keicho tsunami had an Izu–Bonin (outer-rise) source rather than a Nankai Trough source.
steps.quote: Harada et al. (23) suggested that the 1605 earthquake may have had a source in the Izu–Bonin Islands, rather than the Nankai Trough.

steps.action: Compare the Izu–Bonin scenario footprints with Harada et al.'s modeling and with the 1605 record, which is confined to southern Honshu.
steps.quote: Our modeling of great earthquakes from the Izu–Bonin segment of the IBM is in agreement with that of Harada et al. (23)

steps.action: Exclude an Mw 9.0 or larger Izu–Bonin source for 1605, because such a source would have been observed on the northeast Honshu coast.
steps.quote: it is unlikely to have been as large as Mw 9.0

steps.action: Compare South Mariana scenario observability with the absence of Japanese reports of the 1849 Guam tsunami.
steps.quote: Given the apparent lack of tsunami reports from Japan for the 1849 Guam earthquake and tsunami

steps.action: Exclude an Mw 8.7 or larger magnitude for the 1849 Guam earthquake.
steps.quote: [...] the 1849 Guam earthquake must have been less than Mw 8.7

steps.action: Identify gauges especially sensitive to IBM sources (Hilo, Toucheng, Tanabe, Otsuchi) from the model output and attribute them to bathymetric focusing, reflection and resonance (Figures S2, S3).
steps.quote: Both the wave heights at Hilo and the Toucheng appear to be due to focusing of wave energy by undersea bathymetry.

steps.action: State the limits of the tidal-range index (harbour currents, night arrival, low tide, stormy seas) and propose horizontal flow velocity as a future measure.
steps.quote: Our approach to estimating tsunami observability focuses heavily on comparing the predicted tsunami wave heights to the local tidal range.

steps.action: Keep the conditional constraint that, if the written records are complete, the largest IBM earthquake since at least 1605 was smaller than Mw 8.7.
steps.quote: this would constrain the magnitude of the largest earthquake from the Izu–Bonin–Mariana system to less than Mw 8.7 since at least 1605.

end.claim: Assuming written tsunami records at the chosen locations are complete, the largest IBM earthquake since at least 1605 was smaller than Mw 8.7, whereas tsunamis from IBM sources larger than Mw 9.0 would have been visible at many Pacific Basin locations.

decisive_move.sentence: The GeoClaw forward simulations of nine segment-and-magnitude scenarios at historically documented gauges, read through the tidal-range observability index, produce every observability expectation that the bound rests on.

gates.evidence: Action: the observability question, not a stated hypothesis, directed the choice of gauges with long written records (§3 ¶3). Claim: the bounds could have failed had the catalogues contained unexplained far-field tsunamis matching IBM footprints, but the record check is a catalogue reading of earliest dates and completeness onsets (§5 ¶1–5), and the authors disclaim arguing from absence (§5 ¶1). Registration: the thresholds were set from NCEI eyewitness records during the analysis (§3 ¶6); nothing is reported as fixed in advance.

imports.item: GeoClaw finite-volume shallow-water solver with adjoint-guided adaptive mesh refinement
Written historical archives (Japanese, Spanish colonial and other records) and their completeness, preservation and access
Argument from ignorance, used to delimit what absent records can show

novelty_claims.quote: We approach the question from a different point of view: what if the IBM has hosted great earthquakes and no documentable evidence was left?

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Inference: the conclusion's bound of less than Mw 8.7 since 1605 (§7 ¶1) sits uneasily with the paper's own results. Mw 8.7 sources give about half the tidal range at many sites and are 'essentially unobservable' at most locations (§0 ¶1; §4 ¶2), and the per-segment completeness dates (1403, 1611, 1241) differ from 1605 (§5 ¶6–8). The conclusion also hedges that sources smaller than Mw 8.7 would be unobservable, so the bound has no resolution below the scenario grid. The headline status 'estimate_with_resolution' is generous: resolution is the 0.3-Mw scenario spacing, and no uncertainty is quantified. Only one slip distribution per magnitude and segment is modeled, without variation in slip, depth, dip, outer-rise versus megathrust mechanism, or segment-spanning ruptures. The observability thresholds (30%, 100%) rest on three eyewitness cases and are not varied. The historical record is read for earliest dates and completeness onsets, not systematically searched for orphan tsunamis matching IBM footprints. Fig. 4 marks orphan tsunamis (e.g., 1700, 1687, 1730, 1751) but the text does not examine them as IBM candidates. §5 ¶1 explicitly disclaims the absence-of-evidence argument, yet §6.1 and §7 rely on absence of reports. Sub-claims: 1605 Keicho smaller than Mw 9.0 (best_explanation, §6.1 ¶1); 1849 Guam smaller than Mw 8.7 (best_explanation, §6.1 ¶2); sensitive locations from bathymetric focusing (best_explanation from model output, §6.2). The paper never confronts McCaffrey's (2008) Mw 9.2–9.5 and 723/893-year recurrence with its bound. Minor inconsistencies: Fig. 3 row label 'Mw 8.8' versus the caption's Mw 8.7 (p. 8); Atwater et al. 2005, cited in Fig. 4, is not in the reference list; Table 2 contains negative 'maximum' values.

disagreements.target: Chilean–Mariana subduction style classification paradigm (Uyeda and Kanamori 1979; Ruff and Kanamori 1980; Kanamori 1986)
disagreements.support: The paper relies on refutations established by others (Cascadia 1700, Sumatra 2004, Tohoku 2011), not on its own results, which do not test the predicted IBM limit of Mw 7.6.
disagreements.quote: provided direct refutations of the predictions from this classification scheme

disagreements.target: Harada et al. (2013), Izu–Bonin source for the 1605 Keicho tsunami
disagreements.support: The Izu–Bonin scenarios agree with large waves on south Honshu, but predict that an Mw 9.0 or larger source would have been observed on northeast Honshu, where no 1605 record exists, so the event was likely smaller.
disagreements.quote: it is unlikely to have been as large as Mw 9.0

alternatives_considered.chosen: Three fault segments partitioned by large-scale strike
alternatives_considered.reason: Tsunami energy is directed perpendicular to strike; spanning ruptures should show combined directivity, as in the NOAA SIFT approach
Shuto's Eq. (1) predicts negligible dispersion to at least 4000 km

alternatives_considered.chosen: Gauges in water shallower than 20 m
alternatives_considered.reason: To capture shallow-water wave heights while retaining the full waveform

alternatives_considered.chosen: Maximum wave height relative to the mean tidal range as the observability index
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Changes in harbour current speed and direction (horizontal flow velocity), time of arrival, sea state
alternatives_considered.reason: Mean tidal range is a benchmark an observer familiar with local tides might use

alternatives_considered.chosen: Unobservable/Possibly Observable cut-off at 30% of tidal range; Likely Observable above 100%
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Eyewitness minima of 15% (Gisborne 1906) and 89% (Grenada 1867), and records of 0.1 m heights
alternatives_considered.reason: Most 0.1 m entries are marigraph readings; 30% follows the smallest reliable eyewitness observations

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude northern New Guinea (and east Philippines) from the gauges
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Gauges on the north coast of New Guinea and the east coast of the Philippines
alternatives_considered.reason: Presumed lack of a written historical record before the instrumental period
